content: Certain antiretroviral medications, such as rilpivirine (Edurant), nelfinavir (Viracept), or saquinavir (Invirase), which are used to treat HIV or AIDS, may interact with omeprazole. Additionally, St. John’s Wort and rifampin, a medication commonly used to treat tuberculosis, can also interact with omeprazole. Some other medications may alter the blood levels of omeprazole, and omeprazole may similarly affect the blood levels of other drugs. It is essential to inform your healthcare provider about all medications you are currently taking or have recently taken, including prescription drugs, over-the-counter (OTC) medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, and other supplements. Omeprazole can affect the absorption of certain other medications. Therefore, it is crucial to discuss all medications you are taking with your healthcare provider to ensure there are no potential interactions. This list may not include all possible drug interactions with omeprazole. If you or someone else has accidentally taken too much omeprazole, seek medical help immediately. Call 911 or contact a Poison Control Center at 800-222-1222. If you miss a dose of omeprazole, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and take only the next scheduled dose. Do not take double or extra doses to make up for the missed one. The most common side effects of omeprazole include headache, stomach pain, nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, gas, and, in children aged 1 to 16 years, infections in the nose or throat and fever. If any of these side effects bother you, inform your healthcare provider. There may be other side effects not listed here. If you suspect you are experiencing a side effect, contact your healthcare provider or report it to the FDA at 800-FDA-1088 or Health Canada at 866-234-2345. Serious side effects of omeprazole, while less common, include kidney problems such as acute tubulointerstitial nephritis, which can occur at any time during treatment. If you notice a decrease in urine output or blood in your urine, contact your doctor immediately. Antibiotic-associated diarrhea caused by an overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) in the gut can occur during omeprazole treatment. Symptoms include watery diarrhea, persistent diarrhea, blood in the stool, severe stomach cramps, and fever. If you experience these symptoms, contact your healthcare provider immediately. Omeprazole can cause severe skin reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN), which can be life-threatening if untreated. If you develop a rash, stop taking omeprazole and contact your healthcare provider immediately. Seek emergency help if you experience symptoms such as painful red or purple skin that peels, flat red rashes or blisters on the skin, mouth, nose, or genitals, or red, painful, watery eyes. A severe allergic reaction called DRESS (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms) can occur with omeprazole. This reaction can affect multiple organs, including the liver, kidneys, and heart. Symptoms include skin rash or hives, fever, swollen lymph nodes, shortness of breath, swelling in the feet, ankles, or legs, dark-colored urine, or yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice). Stop using omeprazole and seek immediate medical attention if you experience these symptoms. Omeprazole may cause or worsen lupus, an autoimmune disorder where the immune system attacks the body’s own cells and organs. If you develop new or worsening joint pain or a rash on your arms or cheeks, inform your healthcare provider immediately. Long-term use of omeprazole (three years or longer) can lead to vitamin B12 deficiency, as it reduces the absorption of this vitamin. Symptoms of deficiency include a sore tongue, weakness, or tingling and numbness in the hands or feet. If you experience these symptoms, stop using omeprazole and contact your healthcare provider. Omeprazole can cause low magnesium levels (hypomagnesemia), which may result in seizures or heart rhythm problems. People taking omeprazole for a long time or those on other medications that lower magnesium levels are at higher risk. Symptoms include changes in heart rate or rhythm, dizziness, muscle spasms, or seizures. Stop using omeprazole and contact your healthcare provider if you experience these symptoms. Omeprazole may increase the risk of bone loss and fractures, particularly in older adults and those taking high doses or using the medication long-term. If you are concerned about this risk, discuss it with your healthcare provider. Omeprazole can cause serious allergic reactions. Symptoms include breathing problems, wheezing, a racing heart, fever, swollen lymph nodes, swelling of the face, lips, mouth, tongue, or throat, difficulty swallowing, throat tightness, itching, skin rash, hives, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, lightheadedness, fainting, stomach cramps, or joint pain. Stop using omeprazole and seek immediate medical attention if you experience any of these symptoms. People allergic to omeprazole, Prilosec, Prilosec OTC, other proton pump inhibitors, or any ingredients in the specific product should not use omeprazole. Your pharmacist can provide a list of ingredients in the product. Omeprazole should not be taken with certain other medications. Inform your healthcare provider about all prescription and OTC medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, and supplements you are using. This will help them determine if omeprazole is safe for you. Do not take omeprazole unless prescribed by a healthcare provider. Take it exactly as prescribed and do not share it with others, even if they have the same condition. Keep omeprazole out of reach of children. Do not chew, cut, or crush the capsules. Take omeprazole before a meal. Antacids may be taken with omeprazole if needed. If you have difficulty swallowing the capsule, you may open it and sprinkle the contents on one tablespoon of applesauce. Swallow the applesauce immediately without mixing it with other foods. Omeprazole is not intended for immediate relief of heartburn. It may take one to four days for the medication to take full effect. Before using omeprazole, inform your healthcare provider about all your health conditions, including low blood potassium (hypokalemia), low blood magnesium (hypomagnesemia), low blood calcium (hypocalcemia), or liver problems. This information will help your provider determine if omeprazole is appropriate for you. If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, inform your healthcare provider. It is not known if omeprazole can harm an unborn baby. Your provider will advise you on whether to take omeprazole during pregnancy. Do not take omeprazole while breastfeeding, as it can pass into breast milk. Take omeprazole before meals. It is unknown if alcohol consumption affects omeprazole. Always inform your healthcare provider about all medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, and supplements you are using. Certain medications, such as clopidogrel (Plavix), cilostazol (Pletal), citalopram, methotrexate, digoxin (Lanoxin), warfarin, antiretroviral medications (e.g., rilpivirine, nelfinavir, saquinavir), St. John’s Wort, and rifampin, may interact with omeprazole. Discuss these with your provider before starting omeprazole.
